summary: A Riverbend resident reflects on the environmental costs of the Riverbend Flood Barrier, which began construction on October 11, 2023. The essay describes dust, noise, declining birds and water quality, and lost greenspace and trees. It weighs flood safety against ecological harm, quotes local voices, and calls for greener construction and mindful stewardship.
one_line: A Riverbend resident weighs the flood barrier's promised safety against its toll on wildlife, water quality and greenspace, urging greener, more considerate public works.
key_facts: Construction of the Riverbend Flood Barrier began on October 11, 2023, with the first shovel striking the ground.
The author, a lifelong Riverbend resident, wrote the reflection nearly six months into the project.
The project's Environmental Impact Assessment promised minimal disruption, but the author says the promise does not tell the whole story.
On September 20, 2023, the author noticed fewer birds around their feeder.

Local biologist Derek Saunders warned that construction runoff could introduce sediments and pollutants into waterways; the author says the warnings now seem prescient, with fluctuating aquatic life and declining water clarity.
Marjorie Thomson, who operates the local nursery, reports fewer customers wanting to add to their gardens because construction zones encroach on shrinking spaces.
Long-standing trees were felled to build the barriers against floods.
Council debates on December 15, 2023, used terms like "sustainable development" and "climate resilience."
Emma Rodriguez, a climate activist and local teacher, asked for whom a resilient future is being built, saying it shouldn't come at the expense of the natural world.
Community efforts include a tree-planting campaign led by local schools and a water monitoring initiative led by scientists from the Riverbend Research Institute.
James Pinewood, a third-generation Riverbender, said heritage includes the air, water and soil that people inherit and owe forward.
The author has urged city planners to adopt greener construction methods and materials but finds bureaucracy slow.
